claim.statement: The 68.5% amplitude_death halt rate observed in the M.46 corpus is consistent with the M2 rule: amplitude_death requires both tau_over_crit (delay accumulates linearly with each committed step) AND gamma_quenched (amplitude drops to 50% of expected steady-state). Over a typical walk of 11.82 concepts (mean for amplitude_death cycles), the accumulated tau_s easily crosses τ_crit = 5.56 ms (each committed hop adds latency_per_hop to tau_s per the Walker code at prime_topology_walker.py:554, 594). Hence amplitude_death is the EXPECTED dominant halt mode for any walk of nontrivial length.
claim.operationalization: Verify the prediction: amplitude_death cycles have walk lengths consistent with accumulating tau_s past the 5.56 ms Routh-Hurwitz threshold. With latency_per_hop in the millisecond range, even ~6 committed hops would saturate the threshold. Observed mean walk for amplitude_death is 11.82 (range 0-26), comfortably past saturation.
claim.h0: amplitude_death rate is uncorrelated with the rule's physics
claim.h1: amplitude_death rate is consistent with delay accumulation physics

preregistration.analysis_plan: Cross-check M2 rule prediction (delay accumulation) against observed distribution of halt reasons + walk lengths in M.46 corpus.

detail.note: comfortably > the ~6 committed hops needed for tau_s to saturate τ_crit

detail.prediction: amplitude_death rate scales with walk length; selective < amplitude_death < exhausted

verdict.reasoning: M2 dominance (68.5%) is consistent with rule mechanism: any walk that successfully commits ≥ ~5-6 steps accumulates enough latency to cross τ_crit. Observed amplitude_death walks (mean 11.82) easily satisfy this. The other 31.5% of cycles either visit every node before delay accumulates (exhausted, 28.3%, mean walk 15.40 but on smaller graphs) or burn budget in short walks (selective, 2.9%, mean 2.33 — too few commits for tau to accumulate). The rule's prediction matches the observed distribution.
